content: The WHO Guideline Steering Group carefully reviewed the feedback provided and incorporated it into the final document, ensuring that any conflicts of interest among members of the External Review Group were appropriately addressed. Updated recommendations were made regarding HIV prevention, infant diagnosis, initiation of antiretroviral therapy (ART), and monitoring. A simplified diagnostic algorithm for infants was also introduced, focusing on the following principles for determining HIV infection in HIV-exposed infants and children under 18 months of age in lowand middle-income countries: 1. Assessment of HIV exposure: Determine the HIV exposure status of the infant by performing antibody testing on the mother. 2. Nucleic acid testing (NAT): Conduct NAT for any HIV-exposed child presenting with clinical symptoms outside the national infant testing algorithm, regardless of prior NAT results. 3. Testing at nine months: Perform NAT for all HIV-exposed infants, whether symptomatic or asymptomatic, at nine months of age, even if previous NAT results were negative. 4. Indeterminate results: Ensure that indeterminate test results are immediately retested and prioritized for rapid resolution. 5. Confirmatory testing: Conduct confirmatory testing following any positive NAT result. 6. Regular follow-up: Provide regular follow-up for all HIV-exposed infants until a final diagnosis is made. This includes administering co-trimoxazole prophylaxis and conducting clinical and nutritional assessments. Additional notes and considerations: Inclusion of NAT at birth: Based on the 2016 WHO Consolidated ARV Guidelines, adding NAT at birth to the existing testing algorithm can be considered. Point-of-care NAT (POC NAT): POC NAT can be used both to diagnose HIV infection and to confirm positive results. Immediate ART initiation: Start ART without delay if HIV infection is suspected. Simultaneously, retest to confirm the infection. As maternal treatment coverage increases and mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) rates decrease, the likelihood of false-positive results rises. Retesting after an initial positive NAT is therefore critical to avoid unnecessary treatment, especially in settings with lower transmission rates. If the second test is negative, a third NAT should be performed before discontinuing ART. Testing for non-breastfed children: For children who were never breastfed, additional testing following a negative NAT at 4–6 weeks is included in the algorithm to account for potential false-negative results. Risk during breastfeeding: The risk of HIV transmission persists as long as breastfeeding continues. If the nine-month test is conducted less than three months after breastfeeding cessation, infections acquired in the final days of breastfeeding may be missed. Retesting at 18 months or three months after breastfeeding cessation (whichever is later) is necessary for a final assessment of HIV status. Extended breastfeeding: If breastfeeding extends beyond 18 months, the final HIV diagnosis can only be made at the end of breastfeeding. If breastfeeding ends before 18 months, the final diagnosis using antibody testing can only be made at 18 months. Antibody testing should be performed at least three months after breastfeeding cessation to allow for the development of HIV antibodies. Confirmation for infants under 18 months: For infants younger than 18 months, NAT should be performed to confirm HIV infection.
